title: Running a Local LLM on Company Data: What You Actually Need to Know
content_html:
Your finance team handles invoices and contracts that cannot leave your servers. Your compliance officer needs to search through years of audit trails without sending them to a third party. Your operations team processes sensitive client data every day. When you have documents like these, the question becomes simple: can you use a cloud AI assistant, or do you need a local LLM on company data?

The honest answer is that both can work. But they solve different problems, and the choice depends on what your team actually needs.

Why teams choose a local LLM

A local LLM on company data runs inside your own infrastructure. The model reads and searches your documents. It does not train on them, and it does not send them anywhere. For teams handling personal data, financial records, or proprietary information, this matters. A cloud AI assistant under a processing agreement is perfectly fine for many workflows. But if your legal or compliance team has said no to cloud processing, a local setup gives you control over where data lives and who can access it.

The privacy argument is real. It is also the main reason to choose local over cloud.

What a local LLM actually costs you

Running a local LLM on company data is not just downloading software and pressing start. You need suitable hardware. Usually that means a GPU server, not your existing office machines. That server needs to be maintained, updated and monitored. If the model breaks or the hardware fails, someone has to fix it. If a new, better model comes out, you have to evaluate it, test it and deploy it yourself.

This is not a complaint about local AI. It is the trade-off you accept when you want the data to stay local. Cloud AI handles that maintenance for you. Local AI hands it to you.

Comparing model quality

A local LLM on company data performs differently than a cloud AI assistant. Some local models are very good. Others are not. You will need to test the model you choose against your actual documents before you commit. A local model that struggles with your industry terminology or document format will frustrate your team. A cloud assistant might handle it better, even if you prefer local processing. This is not about brand loyalty. It is about what works for your workflow.

The gap between local and cloud models has narrowed in recent years. But it has not closed. Your choice should be based on testing with your own documents, not on promises.

What to look for in a private AI setup

If you decide to run a local LLM on company data, your setup needs to answer these questions. Where does the data live when the model reads it? Who has access to the server and the documents? Is every AI action logged so you can audit what happened? Who maintains the hardware, updates the model and handles failures? Can you recover your data if something goes wrong? These are not optional. They are the difference between a private AI setup that works and one that creates new problems.

Many teams find that a local LLM on company data is the right choice for a specific workflow, not the whole business. Your contracts team might use local AI. Your customer support team might use cloud AI. Both can coexist.

Building and hosting a local LLM

If you decide local is right for you, building it is not a weekend project. You need to define what the AI should do, test it against real documents and set up the infrastructure to run it safely.
